events.description: An engineer starts setting up multiple PostgreSQL servers in the staging environment to try out pgpool-II for load balancing queries (infrastructure#259).

Prior to starting the work, the engineer takes an LVM snapshot of the production database and loads it into the staging environment to get a more up-to-date copy than the automatic daily 01:00 UTC process provides.

GitLab.com begins experiencing a significant increase in database load, suspected to be spam; many users cannot post comments on issues and merge requests, and getting load under control takes several hours.
A background job attempting to remove a GitLab employee's flagged account and associated data contributes to part of the database load.

Due to increased load, the PostgreSQL secondary's replication lags and fails because required WAL segments were already removed from the primary; with no WAL archiving, the secondary must be manually re-synchronised. An engineer wipes the secondary's data directory and runs pg_basebackup, which hangs silently; max_wal_senders is increased from 3 to 32, PostgreSQL fails to restart due to semaphore limits, and max_connections is reduced from 8000 to 2000 before PostgreSQL restarts successfully. pg_basebackup still does not start replication, and strace shows it hanging in a poll call.

An engineer suspects pg_basebackup created files in the secondary's data directory during previous attempts; later it is revealed this is normal behaviour, as pg_basebackup waits silently for the primary to start sending data.

While trying to restore replication, an engineer mistakenly wipes the PostgreSQL data directory on the primary instead of the secondary; the process is terminated a second or two later, but around 300 GB of data has already been removed.
Engineers look for database backups and ask for help on Slack; both finding and using backups fail completely.

The S3 pg_dump backup bucket is found to be empty: the backup procedure ran pg_dump 9.2 on an application server, which defaulted to 9.2 because no PostgreSQL data directory was present, while the database runs 9.6, so pg_dump errored; cronjob failure notifications were rejected by DMARC, so the failures went unnoticed.

Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers; LVM snapshots (one from ~24 hours before, one manually created ~6 hours before the outage) were evaluated, and the 6-hour-old snapshot was chosen to minimise data loss.

Copying the data directory from the staging host to the production host takes around 18 hours due to slow, throttled network disks; the database is restored to its state as of January 31st, 17:20 UTC.
GitLab.com database is restored without webhooks.
Final restoration procedures are completed, including restoring webhooks, and operations are confirmed to be working as expected.
